voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: He is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort were things we laid down to come near him. To the virgin among us he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighed every earthly marriage. To the scholar he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. We held his death to be redemption. His resurrection was the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: He redeemed us by his death and rose from the dead - that is the center. We held that he entered the world as a poor child, was born of the virgin in Bethlehem, and lived the prophets' simplicity. We read those writings as true witness, received from the apostles, though more than three centuries stood between us and the events. Our confidence rested on the apostles' writings as the church received them, on the worship that carried them forward, and on the places themselves - we could walk to the cave of his birth. What he accomplished we spoke of as buying us back with his blood. That is near to later language of punishment in our place, without being identical to it; the exact formula belongs to another age. The resurrection was not background for us - it was the hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: The ordinary word for a male ascetic was monachus - a monk. It is close to the modern word, though our monks - the monachi - at Bethlehem lived under no written rule and belonged to no order as later centuries knew them. The word came to us from Greek, where it meant someone living alone, though our men lived in community. We also spoke of the monasterium, the monastery - at Bethlehem it meant a men's house and a women's house under one project, funded from Paula's fortune. The women lived in three companies that met to pray, and Paula, then Eustochium, led them. But we have no names for the ordinary men who lived there, and no record of their inner life. What we kept was the structure and the word, not the faces.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
We believed it because the writings about Jesus said so, and we trusted those writings enough to spend a lifetime correcting them word by word. Three centuries stood between us and the events. Our confidence rested on three things: the apostles' writings as the church received them, the worship that carried them forward, and the places themselves - we could walk to the cave of the birth. That last one set us apart. Jerome wrote that Paula, standing at that cave, saw the infant in the manger with the eyes of faith: “In my hearing she declared that, with the eyes of faith, she could see the infant Lord wrapped in cloths and crying in the manger. She could see the wise men worshipping him and the star shining overhead. She could see the virgin mother, the watchful foster-father, and the shepherds coming by night.”

The land itself we treated as a kind of witness. And we believed it because the resurrection was a hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it. Paula left Rome, her children standing on the shore. Fabiola sold her property and carried the sick in from the streets. We staked everything on the promise that the treasure is in heaven.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: Paula lived it. Her daughter Blaesilla died young, soon after taking up the ascetic life - the renuntiatio. At the funeral the crowd said fasting had killed her, and asked why these detestable monks were not driven out of Rome, or stoned, or thrown into the Tiber. Paula herself was carried out fainting. Jerome wrote her a letter afterward - an epistula, the form our teaching traveled in - that pardoned a mother's tears and still asked her to hold them back. Years later, when Paula herself died, Jerome wrote her epitaphium, the commemorative letter for the dead that taught the living what a holy life looked like. He told her whole life as an ideal, from her high birth through her choice to leave Rome, her children standing on the shore, to her years leading the women's monasterium at Bethlehem. That letter is what we have of her, and we tell you plainly what it is: a memorial written to teach, not a recording of her voice. The weeping at her daughter's funeral and the idealized life in the epitaphium - we kept both, because both were true.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: We held the firmest convictions, and we suffered anyway. That is what I want you to understand. That is the shaped answer, the one we wrote for others to read. But it was not the only truth we kept. We did not treat certainty as armor against sorrow, or sorrow as proof of weak faith. The old answers - judgment, reward stored up, the dead safe with Christ - did real work for us, and they also failed to stop our weeping. We kept both the answers and the weeping, on purpose, in the same record. That is the thing we would not want you to miss.
